meta.title: Who really said "We must all suffer from one of two pains: the pain of discipline or the pain of regret. The difference is discipline weighs ounces while regret weighs tons"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Jim Rohn’s signature line on discipline. Wikiquote lists it without a citation, and no book, seminar or dated article containing the wording has been located.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We must all suffer from one of two pains: the pain of discipline or the pain of regret. The difference is discipline weighs ounces while regret weighs tons'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Jim Rohn everywhere and sourced nowhere in particular. What is documented, what is not, and why his maxims resist citation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Rohn everywhere, and entirely in keeping with a man who built a career of more than four decades out of one-sentence maxims — but no book, recording or dated article containing this wording has been located. It is the only entry in the Quotes section of Wikiquote’s Jim Rohn page ↗ — a page of 435 characters in total — and it sits there with no source given at all. Quote Investigator, which has examined another saying credited to Rohn, has no article on this one.

source.excerpt: We must all suffer from one of two pains: the pain of discipline or the pain of regret. The difference is discipline weighs ounces while regret weighs tons.
source.trailTitle: What could and could not be established
trail: Wikiquote’s Jim Rohn page ↗ carries this sentence in its main Quotes section. There is no citation beside it, and no Sourced, Attributed or Misattributed subsection on the page — this one line is the entire Quotes section. (A second Rohn line, “Either you run the day or the day runs you”, appears on the page only as an image caption.)

Quote Investigator has no article on this saying: searches of the site for discipline weighs ounces and regret weighs tons return nothing. Its one investigation of a Rohn-credited line is instructive, though — the famous “average of the five people you spend the most time with” reached print in 2005 only after a chain of hearsay QI reconstructs ↗: Jack Canfield had it from Tim Ferriss, who had it from an unidentified caller who credited Rohn. No Rohn source was ever produced for that one either.

The shape of his career explains the difficulty. Rohn gave his first public seminar at the Beverly Hills Hotel in 1963 ↗ and spent the following decades on the seminar circuit, where his material was spoken long before any of it was printed. A line delivered from a stage in, say, 1974 leaves no citable artifact unless somebody was recording.

The one Rohn title with a public catalogue record that could be checked, the Internet Archive’s copy of Seven Strategies for Wealth and Happiness (Prima, 1988) ↗, is lending-restricted: the scan exists but its text is not served, so the book could not be searched for this sentence. Absence of confirmation here is not evidence against the attribution.
source.cutTag: The wording as Wikiquote carries it
source.excerptNote: This is the wording in circulation, reproduced from Wikiquote’s Jim Rohn page ↗, where it appears without a citation. No earlier or differently-worded printing has been identified, so there is nothing here to compare it against — which is precisely the gap this page is reporting.
source.rightsNote: The specific work is unidentified, so no publication date can be pinned to this line — but every plausible source for it is a Rohn seminar or book from 1963 onward, decades after the pre-1931 cutoff for automatic US public domain, and Rohn died in 2009. Treat it as in copyright and quote it as a short attributed excerpt; it is not cleared for reuse as public-domain text.

author.name: Jim Rohn
author.heading: About Jim Rohn
author.bio: Emanuel James Rohn grew up an only child on an Idaho farm, left college after a year, and went into direct selling — making a fortune by 31, losing it by 33, and making another. After his company collapsed in the early 1960s he was asked to speak at his Rotary Club, and that invitation turned into a career of more than four decades: his first public seminar was at the Beverly Hills Hotel in 1963, and he spent the decades after it on stages across the country. He mentored Tony Robbins and Herbalife’s Mark Hughes early on, and Mark Victor Hansen, Jack Canfield and Brian Tracy all credit him as an influence. His work was delivered aloud first and printed second, which is why so many sayings carry his name and so few carry a citation.

context.heading: Why a motivational maxim is so hard to source
lead: Rohn’s corpus was spoken first and written down later, often by other people. He came out of direct selling ↗, was invited to address his Rotary Club after his company folded, and gave his first paid public seminar in 1963; the books and audio programmes followed the stage, not the other way round. Maxims polished over hundreds of live retellings have no first edition, and the version that finally reaches print is whichever one somebody in the audience wrote down.

That is not a reason to doubt the attribution here — the line is his register, and no rival claimant has ever been proposed. It is a reason this page says attributed rather than verified. Rohn mentored Tony Robbins and Mark Victor Hansen among others ↗, and his sayings travelled outward through them by repetition. Repetition is how a quotation becomes famous; it is not how one becomes documented.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote’s Jim Rohn page gives his dates as September 17, 1930 – December 5, 2009 and his full name as Emanuel James Rohn, and its Quotes section lists exactly one entry — "We must all suffer from one of two pains: the pain of discipline or the pain of regret. The difference is discipline weighs ounces while regret weighs tons." — with no citation. The whole page is 435 characters; a second Rohn line, "Either you run the day or the day runs you", appears only as an image caption.

Wikipedia states Rohn was born 17 September 1930 in Yakima, Washington and died 5 December 2009; grew up on a farm in Caldwell, Idaho; left college after one year; gave his first public seminar at the Beverly Hills Hotel in 1963; and mentored Mark R. Hughes and Tony Robbins, with Mark Victor Hansen, Jack Canfield and Brian Tracy crediting him as an influence.

Quote Investigator traces "You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with" to Jack Canfield and Janet Switzer’s 2005 book The Success Principles, where it is a chapter epigraph credited to Jim Rohn, and reconstructs the route as Canfield learning it from Tim Ferriss, who heard it from an unidentified caller who credited Rohn — no Rohn source.

The Internet Archive holds Seven Strategies for Wealth and Happiness by Jim Rohn, dated June 1, 1988, publisher Prima Lifestyles. The item is lending-restricted: its full text (sevenstrategiesf0000jimr_djvu.txt) returns HTTP 403 "Item not available", so the book could not be searched.
